analysis.one_liner: Treats U.S. companies that move their legal home abroad to dodge taxes as still American for tax purposes.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or vote, after being referred there the day it was introduced in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2014 and 2015, some large American companies cut deals to move their legal headquarters to low-tax foreign countries while their operations, management, and shareholders stayed mostly in the United States — a maneuver called a corporate inversion. This bill would have changed the tax code so that after May 8, 2014, such a company is still taxed as an American company if its former U.S. owners hold more than half the stock, or if its top management stays in the United States and it keeps significant U.S. business activity. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, in two ways. First, the money: when a company on paper becomes foreign, its foreign profits can often escape U.S. tax, and that lost revenue either has to be made up by other taxpayers or cut from spending. Keeping inverted companies on the U.S. tax rolls protects that revenue. Second, fairness: the bill's standard is activity-based — if your executives and business stay here, you pay taxes here — so companies that actually move abroad for real reasons keep a clean exception, while paper flips stop paying off.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers and the federal treasury

how_it_helps.text: The bill would treat a foreign corporation that acquires a U.S. company after May 8, 2014 as an inverted (and therefore domestic, U.S.-taxable) corporation if former U.S. shareholders own more than 50% of the stock, or if management and control of the group occurs primarily in the United States and the group has significant domestic business activities.

It defines significant domestic business activities concretely — for example, at least 25% of the group's employees, employee compensation, assets, or income located in the United States — and requires regulations treating management and control as U.S.-based when substantially all top executives making day-to-day strategic, financial, and operational decisions are based in the United States.

It also lowers the existing test so that a deal counts as an inversion when former U.S. shareholders hold 80% or more of the new entity, expanding the range of paper transactions that stay on the U.S. tax rolls.

analysis.who_pays: U.S.-based multinationals that had already inverted or were planning to — companies in the 2014–15 wave in industries like pharmaceuticals and fast food — because deals that would have moved their foreign earnings off the U.S. tax rolls would no longer work. Their shareholders would face higher expected tax on foreign profits.

drawbacks.text: The bill attacks the symptom, not the cause: the U.S. corporate tax system at the time taxed worldwide profits at a high rate, which is what made relocating on paper attractive. The bill changes nothing about the underlying rates or the system, so companies would keep facing an incentive to restructure in whatever way the rules allow.

The bill preserves an exception for corporate groups with substantial business activities in the country where they are organized, so genuinely foreign combinations — including a full sale of a U.S. company to a foreign buyer — would still escape the rules. Some critics argued strict anti-inversion rules can push companies toward outright foreign sales, which moves even more of the company abroad permanently.

A strictly domestic fix has limits: inversions are about where a company files its paperwork, and international tax planning moves faster than any single-country statute, so the revenue gains depend heavily on regulations the Treasury would have to write.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real but modest in scale: closing the most aggressive paper inversions protects tax revenue and basic fairness, at a direct cost to the shareholders of the companies doing them. The honest caveat is that the bill does nothing about the underlying tax structure that made inversions attractive, and it still allows genuinely foreign mergers. Most tax experts agreed a durable fix required broader international tax reform. As a narrow rule change, it was sound; as a solution to the problem, it was partial.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or markup, and sat there until that Congress expired two years later.

narrative.text: Rep. Sander Levin introduced the bill on January 20, 2015, joined as original cosponsors by Reps. Doggett, Slaughter, and Van Hollen.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation.
That referral was the bill's last action: the committee took no further step, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
Eighteen House members cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats; no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The U.S. multinationals that inverted or were weighing inversions came out ahead: the tax advantages of a foreign paper headquarters survived, and the revenue those flips would have kept on the U.S. tax rolls was never collected. Ordinary taxpayers gained nothing from the bill's death; they simply kept carrying the tax base these maneuvers erode.

industries.industry: U.S. multinationals pursuing or having completed corporate inversions
industries.note: The bill would erase the main tax payoff of reincorporating in a low-tax country while keeping operations in the United States, by treating such companies as domestic for tax purposes. Their saving comes out of the federal revenue everyone else's taxes support.

Inverted companies that remain on the U.S. tax rolls keep paying U.S. tax on their profits, protecting revenue that would otherwise be shifted offshore and made up by other taxpayers or spending cuts.
